titre: Cope Had Put the Elasmosaurus Skull at the End of the Tail
accroche: In 1868, Cope reconstructs a marine reptile from Kansas with the head at the tip of a long appendage. It is the neck, and Leidy shows it, in 1870.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1867, a U.S. Army surgeon, Theophilus Turner, discovers bones in a ravine of the Pierre Shale formation, near Fort Wallace, Kansas. He recognizes an “extinct monster” in them and sends the backbone to Philadelphia. Edward Drinker Cope, who describes it, names the animal Elasmosaurus platyurus in 1868.

## A Skeleton Read Backward

In his reconstruction of 1868-1869, Cope draws a marine reptile with a very long tail, and places the skull at the end of it. The long segment he takes for a tail is in fact a neck, which we now know was made up of more than seventy vertebrae. The longest swan-necked reptile thus ends up with its head on backward.

## Leidy's Correction

On March 8, 1870, before the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia, Joseph Leidy declares that Cope described the skeleton in a position inverted from the true one. According to him, the strange shape of the vertebral joints, which Cope had explained by a second set of articular processes as in snakes, makes sense when one looks at the other end of the backbone, where the axis and atlas are fused: that is where the head was. Leidy counts about seventy-two cervical vertebrae, for a neck of about twenty-two feet, that is, nearly seven meters. He also corrects his own error, made nineteen years earlier, on other vertebrae that he had assigned to the genus Cimoliasaurus. Leidy adds that Elasmosaurus is probably identical to another marine reptile, Discosaurus, which Cope refuses to accept. Cope then tries to withdraw the copies of his preprint and publishes a corrected reconstruction in 1870, with the head at the end of the neck, partly blaming his mistake on Leidy's 1851 error on the Cimoliasaurus vertebrae.

## Who Spotted the Error, and Why the Legend Is Wrong

Tradition often has it that Othniel Charles Marsh, Cope's great rival in the “Bone Wars,” spotted the mistake. The sources consulted indicate that the public correction came from Leidy, Cope's former teacher. Marsh, on the other hand, exploited the error for decades. Paleontologist Jane Davidson, in a 2002 article, judges that Cope should have avoided it, the literature on plesiosaurs being available at the time. She suggests that he repeated it even after it was pointed out to him.

repere.texte: On March 8, 1870, Leidy declares to the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia that Cope described Elasmosaurus in an inverted position, and counts about 72 cervical vertebrae, for a neck of about 22 feet.
repere.source: Leidy, Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia, 22, 1870, pp. 9-10

carte.punch: Cope had placed the skull of a marine reptile at the end of what he thought was its tail.
carte.idee: In 1868, the reconstruction of Elasmosaurus puts the head at the end of an outsized tail. It is in fact a neck of more than seventy vertebrae. Leidy sets the record straight before the Philadelphia Academy on March 8, 1870.

quiz.question: How was Cope's error on Elasmosaurus caught in 1870?
choix: Marsh spots it in a preprint and points it out to Cope
A new discovery in Kansas reveals a skull facing the other way
Leidy points out to the Philadelphia Academy that the skeleton is described backward
Cope corrects it alone by comparing his animal to a snake
quiz.explication: It was Leidy who, on March 8, 1870, pointed out that the skeleton was described in an inverted position, relying on the atlas and axis fused at the other end. Marsh exploited the error without revealing it, no new discovery is involved, and the comparison with snakes was precisely Cope's mistake.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What name does Edward Drinker Cope give the animal in 1868, according to the entry?
choix: Elasmosaurus longicollis, for its long neck
Elasmosaurus platyurus, with its broad tail
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Cope names the animal Elasmosaurus platyurus in 1868. Cimoliasaurus and Discosaurus are other genera, and Elasmosaurus longicollis is not the name Cope gave.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who discovers the first bones of Elasmosaurus, and in what year, according to the entry?
choix: Edward Drinker Cope, in 1868, the year he names it
Theophilus Turner, in 1867, near Fort Wallace
Joseph Leidy, in 1870, in a preprint
Othniel Charles Marsh, in 1851, in a ravine
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the surgeon Theophilus Turner who finds the bones in 1867 in a ravine near Fort Wallace, Kansas. Cope then describes them, and Leidy steps in only in 1870.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the entry say about Davidson's (2002) interpretation of Cope's error?
choix: That it was unavoidable for lack of complete skeletons
That it came from Marsh, who had spread it first
That it was corrected by Cope as early as 1868
That it was hard to explain given the available literature
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry reports that Davidson judges the error hard to explain, the literature on plesiosaurs being available. Cope even repeated it after it was pointed out to him, which contradicts the idea of a correction in 1868.
